contents.human: The findings of this study highlight the utility of directed functional connectivity (dFC) as a robust biomarker for understanding the neural mechanisms underlying motor skill learning and retention. By capturing the dynamic neural adaptations that occur during the acquisition of complex motor skills, dFC provides insights beyond traditional performance metrics, offering a comprehensive view of the learning process. The results revealed distinct neural patterns associated with different stages of the Fitts and Posner model, underscoring the progressive refinement of motor control circuits as participants transitioned from the cognitive to the associative stage. Additionally, the study demonstrated the stability of dFC patterns over an extended washout period, suggesting that neural adaptations associated with skill learning are well-retained. These findings have important implications for designing personalized, brain-based training protocols to optimize motor skill acquisition and retention, particularly in fields requiring high precision, such as surgical education. Below, we discuss the significance of these results, their alignment with existing literature, and the broader implications for skill acquisition research. The large difference in post-training and expert brain connectivity (S. Figure 5) indicates that trainees did not reach the autonomous stage. This outcome can be attributed to two key factors that likely influenced the depth of skill acquisition. First, the complexity of the suturing with intracorporeal knot-tying task likely demands prolonged and intensive training to achieve the autonomous stage. Unlike simpler motor tasks that may lead to automation within hours or weeks of practice, mastering complex surgical skills often requires months of dedicated effort[82][83]. Second, the observed differences in brain connectivity suggest that the neural adaptations associated with skill automation had not fully developed within the training period of this study. Neural adaptation involves refining motor control circuits and reducing reliance on higher-order cognitive processes, which typically occur over extended practice. Together, these findings underscore the need for longer training durations and more repetitions to achieve the autonomous stage in complex tasks like this, where precision and coordination are paramount. The dFC-based CPD analysis identified the transition from the cognitive to the associative stage on the sixth day of training for most of the subtasks, while behavioral metrics indicated this transition on the fifth day. This temporal discrepancy suggests a potential lag between observable performance improvements and underlying neuroplastic changes. The delay may be attributed to motor memory consolidation during sleep or rest periods following the training on the fifth day. Consolidation not only cements neural processes but also enhances them[28]. The “one-day“ delay aligns with the time typically needed for sleep-dependent consolidation processes to occur[28]. This finding aligns with other studies that have observed delayed neuroplasticity or neural processes following motor skill training[35][84][85], which is speculated to relate to the fine-tuning of movement patterns, leading to reduced energy and metabolic costs[86]. The variation in transition days between subtasks (sixth day for most and third day for ST13, S. Figure 2) suggests that motor learning unfolds over different timescales for different subtasks and dFCs[87][22]. The dFC results can be used in conjunction with behavioral metrics to provide a more comprehensive understanding of skill acquisition. The early transition on the third day for subtask ST13 provided extended time for neural adaptation in the associative stage, making it the most differentiating subtask between preand post-training days, with a high classification accuracy of 94.4%. The initial rapid improvement of performance in the cognitive stage, followed by a gradual gain in the associative stage (Figure 8 (a) and (b)) aligns with the typical learning curve reported by other studies that are consistent with the Fitts and Posner model[23][88][89]. Early gains likely result from initial task comprehension and strategy formation, while later gains reflect refined motor control through practice. Both online[90] and offline[91][92](i.e. the resting period between trials) learning may have contributed to the observed continuous improvement. The high-performance metrics (accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, MCC, and AUC) achieved by the classifiers (Table 1) in distinguishing preand post-training dFC patterns underscore the efficacy of dFC as a biomarker of motor skill learning. The observed difference is due to the neural adaptation induced by motor skill learning on progressing from the start of the cognitive to the end of the associative stage[16][24][93]. High neural adaptation was observed during specific subtasks (ST3, ST4, ST6, ST8, and ST13), likely due to their complexity, requiring greater cognitive and motor adjustments compared to simpler subtasks. These findings are consistent with previous studies[24][94][95] that reported neural adaptations associated with the acquisition of new motor skills. The lack of neural adaptation in the control group (S. Table 4) confirms that the dFC changes in the learning group were specifically induced by motor training, rather than external factors such as task familiarity or incidental exposure. This supports the specificity of dFC as a sensitive and reliable biomarker of motor learning. The gradual decrease in strength of highly adapted dFCs from preto post-training (Figure 6 and S. Figure 2) is consistent with Hebb’s law[96], which posits that that repeated activation of neurons during training leads to more efficient communication[97], reducing the overall strength of information flow[98]. This observation aligns with other studies[99][100][97][101][102][103][35] that observed a decrease in connectivity strength as a result of neural adaptation[104], which increases efficiency in neural circuits[102][101][105]. For instance, Deeny et al reported a decrease in alpha-band coherence between motor planning and visuospatial attention regions in highly skilled performers[106]. Moreover, motor training reduces the overall excitability threshold of the motor cortex[107], thus requiring less information from the source brain region. Yet it should be noted that the increase or decrease in strength of connectivity is highly task-specific and associated cognitive demands[108]. The correlation between dFC adaptations and behavioral improvements in performance scores (Figure 8(a) and(b)) indicates that dFC is directly associated with performance gains. The adaptation likely lead to the observed reduction in the variability in task duration which is considered the hallmark of skill learning[90]. Further, we observed that group-level neural adaptation is reflected at the individual level (Figure 7 and S. Figure 4), making it a reliable biomarker for tracking individual progress. For instance, if connectivity remains high, it may indicate that the trainee is struggling or not consolidating skills efficiently, providing a quantifiable biomarker for identifying when intervention is necessary. This insight can be leveraged to design personalized training protocols with targeted interventions to enhance the training. Thus, dFC can serve as a biomarker for real-time feedback, enabling trainers to adjust the intensity, duration, and brain stimulation[109][110], or focus on specific subtasks based on individual neural adaptation patterns. Such tailored interventions ensure that each trainee receives customized support to optimize their learning trajectory. The HTA identified key subtasks at which the adaptation of dFC occurred. For instance, in subtask 3, LPFC → SMA, LPMC → RPFC, and RPMC → LPFC were the highly adapted dFCs from preto post-training (Figure 4(a)). The presence of multiple dFCs suggests the integration of various neural mechanisms that collectively contribute to motor skill learning[111]. In this subtask, the participants need to orient the needle (held with one hand) perpendicular to the Penrose drain (held with the other hand). The role of LPFC is to generate motor plans, and cognitive control for motor outputs which are transferred to the SMA, responsible for the generation and coordination of sequential motor tasks[112] and their timing for aligning the needle perpendicular to the Penrose drain. Research has shown that motor learning involves the LPFC → SMA, particularly during the early stages of learning, where higher-order cognitive processes are needed to organize movements into coherent sequences[1][103]. The observed adaptation is likely due to the difference in top-down control of LPFC in the cognitive and associative stages[113]. LPMC and RPMC receive sensory feedback from effectors[114][115] regarding the current position of the needle which is transferred to the prefrontal cortex (RPFC and LPFC) to update the cognitive plan and to orient the needle to be perpendicular to the Penrose drain while holding the Penrose drain with another hand[116]. Here, the sensory feedback helps in real-time adjustment[117]. These adapted connectivities likely reflect an improvement in the integration of sensory feedback (from the RPMC and LPMC) and cognitive control processes (to LPFC and RPFC), enabling efficient control of the needle’s orientation with increasing experience [118]. This observation aligns with the dorsal stream theory of visuomotor control[103][119], where feedback from the motor regions is processed by the prefrontal cortex to guide adjustments based on somatic feedback. Overall, the observed adaptation aligns with the participants progressing through different stages of motor learning[23], with the brain regions being recruited differently[120]. In subtask 4, while piercing the needle into the Penrose drain, SMA → RPFC (Figure 4(b)) was the highly adapted connectivity between the cognitive and associative stages. The SMA, involved in the timing and coordination of fine motor movements, sends feedback to the RPFC[121], which plays a key role in spatial attention (to locate and focus on the marks on the Penrose drain) and monitoring the accuracy of the needle’s trajectory and timed application of the force required to pierce the stretched drain[122][123]. In subtask 6, while tying the knot, one of the highly adapted connectivities, i.e. RPFC → SMA (Figure 4(c)) transfers the attention and strategic plan to the SMA for coordination of motor actions[121]. The second connectivity i.e. SMA → LPMC links cognition to movement[124][125]. It facilitates the transfer of motor sequences to the motor region[126] for execution while tying the knot. Subsequently, the LPMC directs specific motor commands, such as motor angle and required muscle forces, to the hands via the corticospinal tract, to ensure accurate execution of the movement. The third connectivity RPMC → LPFC reflects the difference in sensory feedback dominantly from the hands to the LPFC for planning and cognitive control[127]. In subtask 8, while tying a single throw knot involved two adaptive dFCs: LPFC → LPMC and LPFC → RPFC (Figure 4(d)). The connectivity LPFC → LPMC is essential to transferrin motor plans to the motor region[128][129] for the precise execution required in manipulating the thread with precision to form the knot. Simultaneously, the connectivity LPFC → RPFC transfers the motor plans to the RPFC for spatial attention[130] to crucial environment cues to carefully manage the orientation and positioning of the thread while tying the knot. The RPMC → SMA and SMA → LPMC (Figure 4(e)) were the adaptive connectivities in subtask 13, which involves cutting both ends of the suture. RPMC receives sensory inputs from the somatosensory region[131] and transfers them to the SMA for coordinating, timing, and sequencing the motor actions for precise motor control and the overall coordination of cutting. Simultaneously, the SMA’s communication with the LPMC underscores the need for precise control and timing of right-hand movements, which are crucial for properly orienting the scissors, holding the suture and executing the cut. This connectivity aligns with the SMA’s known role in coordinating complex bimanual tasks[126]. The absence of differences in dFC for any subtask between the last day of the associative stage (i.e. post-training) and the retention day (S. Table 5) suggests that neural adaptations are maintained over the six-week washout period (see strength of connectivities on post-training and retention days in Figure 6 and S. Figure 2, and the statistical test (p > 0.01) in “Evaluation of motor skill retention“ section), indicating successful consolidation. This stability is supported by consistent performance scores between post-training and retention days (Table 3, row 3 and the statistical test (p > 0.01) in “Evaluation of motor skill learning with FLS score“ section), underscoring dFC’s potential as a reliable biomarker for long-term motor skill retention. The observed retention may be attributed to the successful consolidation of the adapted neural interactions[132][133][134]. These findings suggest that once learners transition from the cognitive to the associative stage, the learned motor skills become ingrained at a neural level, allowing for sustained performance without substantial skill decay[28]. However, clear differences in dFCs were observed between pre-training and retention (Table 2) for several subtasks. The differentiating subtasks were similar to that of the learning (i.e. preversus post-training) analysis (see Table 1 and Table 2, except ST 4), further supporting the similarity in dFC between post-training and retention day and consequently the stability of the adapted dFCs from the end of training to the retention day. The difference is reflected in the performance score (Table 3, row 2) which also shows clear differences in pre-training and retention. Interleaved training in this study may have facilitated successful retention, as corroborated by previous studies [36]. Research on motor skill consolidation has consistently shown that rest periods or sleep significantly enhance the retention of newly acquired motor skills[135]. Sleep-dependent mechanisms, such as spindle oscillations[136][137], may have played a key role in this process by facilitating neural consolidation and stabilization of the learned skill. These findings emphasize the importance of rest following active practice in facilitating consolidation which is important for long-term motor skill retention. Analysis of retained dFCs further identified key connectivities supporting long-term skill retention. For instance, in subtask 3 (orienting the needle), the adaptation of LPMC → LPFC connectivity (Figure 9(a)) supports the consolidation of motor skill learning[129][104]. Various studies have reported that the PMC is involved in the storage of motor memory[138] and retention of learned movements [139][140][141], which is transferred to LPFC for cognitive control [57][142] during the orientation task. Similarly, the bimanual coordination observed in tying a double throw knot in subtask 6 is facilitated by RPMC→LPMC connectivity (Figure 9(b))[143], suggesting that interhemispheric communication[144], mediated by the corpus callosum[145][146], supports motor skill retention. In subtask 8 while tying a single throw knot, SMA → RPMC (Figure 9(c)) was the highly adapted connectivity, and in subtask 13 while cutting both ends of the suture, RPMC → SMA (Figure 9(d)) was the highly adaptive connectivity. Tying a knot and cutting the suture involves a sequence of precisely coordinated hand movements. These findings align with the established roles of the SMA and PMC: SMA is essential for timing, initiation, and motor sequencing[147][148][149], while PMC plays a key role in the acquisition, storage, and retrieval of motor memory[117][150][131] necessary for the precise movements. While this study demonstrates dFC’s potential as a biomarker for motor skill learning and retention, some limitations warrant consideration. First, the relatively small sample size limits the generalizability of the findings, and future studies should include larger and more diverse populations to strengthen the validity and applicability of the results. Additionally, while the training duration encompassed key learning stages, a longer training period and extended follow-up are necessary to understand the complete motor skill acquisition process, stages and to evaluate retention beyond the initial six-week period. Another limitation is the specificity of the brain region selection; future studies should incorporate a more detailed selection of brain regions, including subcortical areas such as the cerebellum, striatum, and basal ganglia, which are known to play significant roles in motor coordination, procedural learning, and retention[120][151].
contents.AI: The results from this investigation illuminate the promise of directed functional connectivity (dFC) as a solid biomarker for exploring the neural underpinnings associated with the learning and retention of motor skills. By effectively capturing the adaptive neural changes that transpire during the acquisition of intricate motor skills, dFC offers a deeper level of understanding that transcends conventional performance metrics, thus presenting a holistic overview of the learning phenomenon. The findings unveiled specific neural patterns that correlate with various stages of the Fitts and Posner model, emphasizing the progressively enhanced refinement of motor control circuits as individuals transitioned from the cognitive stage to the associative stage. Furthermore, the study illustrated that dFC patterns remained stable even over an extended washout duration, indicating that the neural adaptations linked to skill acquisition are substantially retained. These insights are significant for the development of customized, brain-based training programs aimed at maximizing both the acquisition and retention of motor skills, especially in domains characterized by a need for precision, such as surgical education. In the subsequent sections, we will delve into the implications of these results, their congruence with existing academic literature, and the wider significance for research in skill acquisition. The pronounced difference in brain connectivity observed between the post-training and expert conditions (see S. Figure 5) suggests that the trainees had not fully reached the autonomous stage in their skill development. This outcome can be attributed to two primary factors that likely affected the depth of skill acquisition. Firstly, the intricate nature of tasks involving suturing and intracorporeal knot-tying necessitates extended and rigorous training to attain the autonomous stage. In contrast to simpler motor tasks that may allow for automation within mere hours or weeks of practice, the mastery of advanced surgical techniques often involves months of concentrated effort[82][83]. Secondly, the identified variances in brain connectivity imply that the neural adaptations related to skill automation had not yet fully matured within the scope of the training conducted in this study. Neural adaptation entails the refinement of motor control circuits alongside a diminished reliance on higher-order cognitive functions, modifications that generally occur over prolonged practice periods. Taken together, these findings reinforce the necessity for longer training durations coupled with more repetitions to facilitate the achievement of the autonomous stage in complex tasks of this nature, where precision and coordinated execution are of utmost importance. The dFC-based cognitive performance diagnostic (CPD) analysis determined that for the majority of subtasks, the transition from the cognitive to the associative stage was evident on the sixth day of training; however, behavioral metrics indicated this transition occurring on the fifth day. This temporal disparity points to a potential lag between measurable performance improvements and neuroplastic changes at a neural level. Such a delay may be attributed to the processes of motor memory consolidation that unfold during sleep or recovery periods following the training session on the fifth day. This consolidation not only solidifies neural pathways but also enhances them[28]. The observed “one-day“ delay is consistent with the typical duration required for sleep-related consolidation processes to take effect[28]. These observations align with other research indicating that neuroplasticity or shifts in neural function may occur after motor skill training [35][84][85], which is speculated to pertain to the meticulous adjustment of movement patterns leading to a decrease in energy and metabolic expenditures[86]. The differences in the days taken to transition between subtasks (the sixth day for most compared to the third day for ST13, S. Figure 2) imply that motor learning evolves over diverse timescales contingent upon the specific subtasks and the corresponding dFCs involved[87][22]. The dFC results and behavioral metrics can be integrated to furnish a more holistic comprehension of skill acquisition progress. The early transition to the associative stage on the third day for subtask ST13 allowed for additional time for neural adaptation during this developmental phase, making it a particularly distinguishing subtask between preand post-training days, achieving an impressive classification accuracy of 94.4%. The pattern of rapid performance improvements in the cognitive stage initially, followed by a steady enhancement during the associative stage (illustrated in Figure 8 (a) and (b)), is consistent with the typical learning curve documented in previous studies that adhere to the Fitts and Posner model[23][88][89]. Early advancements in performance likely stem from heightened understanding of the task dynamics and the establishment of strategic frameworks, whereas subsequent enhancements reflect the refinement of motor control processes through practice. Both online[90] and offline[91][92] learning-meaning the resting periods inserted between trials-were likely contributory factors to the continuous performance enhancements noted. The classifiers showcased high performance metrics (accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, MCC, and AUC) in distinguishing between preand post-training dFC patterns, further emphasizing the effectiveness of dFC as a viable biomarker of motor skill learning. The distinctions observed are fundamentally linked to the neural adjustments induced through motor skill training, transforming throughout the transition from the outset of the cognitive stage to the conclusion of the associative stage[16][24][93]. Strong neural adaptations were observed in relation to specific subtasks (ST3, ST4, ST6, ST8, and ST13), likely resulting from their complexity, which necessitated greater cognitive and motor calibrations compared to simpler tasks. These observations correspond with earlier research[24][94][95] that documented neural adjustments intertwined with the acquisition of novel motor skills. The failure to observe neural adaptations in the control group (see S. Table 4) substantiates that the changes in dFC within the learning group were attributable to the motor training they underwent, rather than being influenced by extraneous factors such as familiarity with the task or incidental exposure to the practice. This strengthens the assertion that dFC serves as a sensitive and trustworthy biomarker for evaluating motor learning processes. The progressive reduction in the intensity of highly adapted dFCs from preto post-training (see Figure 6 and S. Figure 2) aligns harmoniously with Hebb’s law[96], which posits that recurrent neuronal activation throughout training yields more efficient neural communication[97], thereby diminishing the overall strength of information transmission[98]. This has been corroborated by a variety of other studies[99][100][97][101][102][103][35] that have documented a deceleration in connectivity strength as a consequence of neural adaptation[104], promoting heightened efficiency within neural circuits[102][101][105]. For instance, Deeny et al. identified a reduction in alpha-band coherence between the regions responsible for motor planning and visuospatial attention among highly skilled performers[106]. Moreover, motor training results in a decrease in the overall excitability threshold of the motor cortex[107], thereby necessitating less input from the originating brain regions. Nevertheless, it is crucial to recognize that alterations in connectivity strength-whether increases or decreases-are highly task-dependent and closely tied to the cognitive demands involved[108]. The correlation established between dFC adaptations and improvements in performance metrics (displayed in Figure 8(a) and (b)) suggests a direct association between dFC and enhancements in performance. Such adaptations likely facilitated the noted decrease in variability in task duration, which is often recognized as a hallmark of proficiency in skill acquisition[90]. Furthermore, our observations indicated that collective neural adaptations at the group level are observable at the individual level as well (as illustrated in Figure 7 and S. Figure 4), affirming its role as an effective biomarker for tracking individual progress. For example, consistent high connectivity may signal that a trainee is either encountering difficulties or failing to consolidate their skills effectively, thereby providing a quantifiable biomarker to pinpoint when intervention might be necessary. This understanding could be harnessed to develop personalized training protocols enriched with targeted interventions aimed at enhancing overall training effectiveness. Consequently, dFC could function as a real-time feedback biomarker, enabling trainers to adapt the intensity, duration, and specific brain stimulation approaches[109][110], or to concentrate on selected subtasks based on each individual’s neural adaptation trajectories. Such tailored interventions guarantee that every trainee receives individualized guidance to refine their learning path. The hierarchical task analysis (HTA) pinpointed essential subtasks where adaptation of dFC was observed. For example, in subtask 3, LPFC → SMA, LPMC → RPFC, and RPMC → LPFC emerged as highly adapted dFCs from preto post-training (refer to Figure 4(a)). The existence of multiple dFCs signals the integration of myriad neural mechanisms that collectively aid in the learning of motor skills[111]. During this subtask, participants are required to align the needle (held by one hand) perpendicularly to the Penrose drain (held by the other hand). Here, the LPFC plays a pivotal role in formulating motor plans and exercising cognitive control over motor outputs, subsequently relaying these plans to the SMA, which is responsible for generating and synchronizing sequential motor tasks[112] and their timing to ensure the needle’s proper alignment. Previous studies have demonstrated that the motor learning process is marked by interactions between the LPFC and SMA, especially during the earlier phases of learning when higher-level cognitive strategies are essential for organizing movements into cohesive sequences[1][103]. The observed adaptations are likely linked to variations in top-down control exerted by the LPFC during cognitive and associative stages[113]. Both LPMC and RPMC receive sensory feedback about the current position of the needle from the effectors[114][115], which is then conveyed to the prefrontal cortex (RPFC and LPFC) to update the cognitive plan and ensure the needle’s perpendicular orientation to the Penrose drain while the other hand holds the drain[116]. Within this context, sensory feedback is crucial for real-time navigation and adjustments[117]. These adapted connectivity patterns likely symbolize an improved integration of sensory feedback (received from RPMC and LPMC) alongside cognitive control processes (regarding LPFC and RPFC), thereby facilitating effective control over the needle’s orientation as participants gain experience[118]. This observation supports the dorsal stream theory pertaining to visuomotor control[103][119], wherein feedback from motor regions is processed by the prefrontal cortex to govern adjustments based on somatic input. Collectively, the observed adaptations resonate with the evolution of participants through the various phases of motor learning[23], with distinct brain regions being recruited differently[120]. In subtask 4, while penetrating the needle into the Penrose drain, SMA → RPFC (refer to Figure 4(b)) emerged as the highly adapted connectivity bridging the cognitive and associative stages. The SMA, crucial for coordinating fine motor movements as well as managing timing, sends feedback to the RPFC[121], which primarily oversees spatial attention (to locate and emphasize visual marks on the Penrose drain) and monitors the accuracy of the needle’s trajectory, alongside the meticulous timing of the force applied to pierce the stretched drain[122][123]. In subtask 6, which involves knot-tying, a notable adapted connectivity was observed between RPFC → SMA (Figure 4(c)), transferring focus and strategic plans to the SMA to orchestrate motor actions[121]. The second substantial connection, SMA → LPMC, serves to link cognitive processes to physical movement[124][125], facilitating the transference of motor sequences to the motor cortex for execution while tying the knot. Subsequently, LPMC directs precise motor commands-such as the requisite angle and muscular force-to the hands via the corticospinal tract, ensuring accurate completion of the task. The third connectivity, RPMC → LPFC, reflects the integration of sensory feedback predominantly flowing from the hands to the LPFC, which is involved in planning and cognitive oversight[127]. In subtask 8, as while tying a single throw knot, two adaptive dFCs were identified: LPFC → LPMC and LPFC → RPFC (Figure 4(d)). The LPFC → LPMC connectivity is vital for transmitting motor plans to the motor region[128][129] necessary for the precision essential in manipulating the thread to form the knot accurately. At the same time, the LPFC → RPFC connection communicates motor plans to the RPFC, which prioritizes spatial attention[130] towards essential environmental cues, thereby enabling a deft management of the thread’s orientation and positioning throughout the knot-tying process. In subtask 13, pertaining to cutting both ends of the suture, the RPMC → SMA and SMA → LPMC pathways (Figure 4(e)) were notable adaptive connectivities. RPMC acquires sensory data from the somatosensory area[131] and conveys this information to the SMA, which allows for the coordination, timing, and sequencing of motor actions needed for precise motor control and overall cutting coordination. Furthermore, SMA’s communication with LPMC reinforces the critical nature of precise control and timing of right-hand movements, which are vital for effectively positioning the scissors, holding the suture, and executing the cut. This connectivity aligns with the established role of the SMA in orchestrating complex bi-manual tasks[126]. The absence of any distinguishable differences in dFC for every subtask between the final day of the associative stage (post-training) and the retention evaluation (see S. Table 5) indicates that the neural adaptations were maintained throughout the six-week washout period (inferred from the strength of connectivities assessed on both post-training and retention days illustrated in Figure 6 and S. Figure 2, coupled with statistical findings [p > 0.01] detailed in the “Evaluation of motor skill retention“ section). This finding suggests effective consolidation of skills. Such stability is corroborated by consistent performance metrics recorded from post-training to retention days (reflected in Table 3, row 3 and statistical assessments [p > 0.01] detailed in the “Evaluation of motor skill learning with FLS score“ section), highlighting the potential of dFC as a dependable biomarker for the sustained retention of motor skills. The identified retention could be attributed to the triumphant consolidation of the neural engagements adapted during training[132][133][134]. These insights indicate that once learners successfully transition from the cognitive to the associative stage, the motor skills acquired become ingrained at a neural level, allowing for continuity in performance without significant skill degradation[28]. Nevertheless, marked disparities in dFCs were evident when comparing pre-training conditions to retention for several subtasks, as laid out in Table 2. The subtasks that distinguished themselves were analogous to those evidenced in the learning (i.e., pre-vs post-training) analysis (see Tables 1 and 2, with the exception of ST 4), thus further reinforcing the parallels in dFC between post-training and retention evaluations and thereby validating the stability of the adjusted dFCs from the conclusion of training to retention. This discrepancy was also apparent in the performance scoring (Table 3, row 2), which displayed clear differences between pre-training and retention contexts. The use of interleaved training within this study likely served to facilitate effective skill retention, corroborating findings from previous research [36]. Investigations into the mechanisms of motor skill consolidation have consistently illustrated that employing rest periods or sleep significantly optimizes the retention of newly acquired skills[135]. Sleep-dependent processes-such as spindle oscillations[136][137]-could have been instrumental in this phenomenon, aiding in the consolidation and stabilization of the learned skills. These findings underscore the critical importance of rest following active practice sessions in promoting consolidation, which is essential for long-term retention of motor skills. The analysis of retained dFCs also uncovered significant connectivities that bolster long-term skill retention. For instance, in subtask 3 (pertaining to the orientation of the needle), the adaptation of LPMC → LPFC connectivity (Figure 9(a)) reinforces the notion that this pathway supports the consolidation of motor skill learning[129][104]. Multiple studies have indicated that the PMC is central to the preservation of motor memory[138] and the retention of learned motor sequences[139][140][141], transferring this information to the LPFC for cognitive management during the task of needle orientation. Similarly, the coordination observed in tying a double throw knot during subtask 6 is supported by the RPMC → LPMC connectivity (Figure 9(b))[143], indicating that interhemispheric communication[144], facilitated by the corpus callosum[145][146], plays a role in fostering motor skill retention. In subtask 8, which involved tying a single throw knot, the SMA → RPMC (Figure 9(c)) connectivity was identified as a crucial adaptive pathway, while in subtask 13 (cutting both ends of the suture), the RPMC → SMA pathway (Figure 9(d)) was highlighted as particularly adaptive. Both tying knots and cutting sutures necessitate a synchronized series of hand movements executed with precision. Collectively, these observations correspond with the recognized functions of the SMA and PMC: the SMA is pivotal for timing, initiation, and the sequencing of motor actions[147][148][149], while the PMC is essential for the acquisition, preservation, and retrieval of motor memory[117][150][131], all of which are critical for achieving the requisite precision in movement execution. While this study effectively demonstrates the potential of dFC as a biomarker for the learning and retention of motor skills, certain limitations merit attention. The relatively small sample size poses challenges to the generalizability of these findings; thus, future research endeavors should aim to encompass larger, more diverse cohorts to augment the validity and applicability of the results. Additionally, although the training duration encapsulated key stages of learning, extending both the training period and follow-up durations would be beneficial for comprehensively understanding the motor skill acquisition process and its stages, as well as evaluating skill retention beyond the initial six-week timeframe. Another aspect to consider is the specificity concerning the selection of brain regions; therefore, future research should entail a more nuanced selection of regions, incorporating subcortical structures such as the cerebellum, striatum, and basal ganglia, all of which are recognized for their significant contributions to motor coordination, procedural learning, and overall retention[120][151].

name of paper: Benchmarking Multimodal RAG through a Chart-based Document Question-Answering Generation Framework
summary: Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (MRAG) enhances reasoning capabilities by integrating external knowledge. However, existing benchmarks primarily focus on simple image-text interactions, overlooking complex visual formats like charts that are prevalent in real-world applications. In this work, we introduce a novel task, Chart-based MRAG, to address this limitation. To semi-automatically generate high-quality evaluation samples, we propose CHARt-based document question-answering GEneration (CHARGE), a framework that produces evaluation data through structured keypoint extraction, crossmodal verification, and keypoint-based generation. By combining CHARGE with expert validation, we construct Chart-MRAG Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for chart-based MRAG evaluation, featuring 4,738 question-answering pairs across 8 domains from real-world documents. Our evaluation reveals three critical limitations in current approaches: (1) unified multimodal embedding retrieval methods struggles in chart-based scenarios, (2) even with ground-truth retrieval, state-of-the-art MLLMs achieve only 58.19% Correctness and 73.87% Coverage scores, and (3) MLLMs demonstrate consistent text-over-visual modality bias during Chart-based MRAG reasoning. The CHARGE and Chart-MRAG Bench are released at this https URL.

name of paper: LServe: Efficient Long-sequence LLM Serving with Unified Sparse Attention
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable potential in processing long sequences, yet efficiently serving these long-context models remains challenging due to the quadratic computational complexity of attention in the prefilling stage and the large memory footprint of the KV cache in the decoding stage. To address these issues, we introduce LServe, an efficient system that accelerates long-sequence LLM serving via hybrid sparse attention. This method unifies different hardware-friendly, structured sparsity patterns for both prefilling and decoding attention into a single framework, where computations on less important tokens are skipped block-wise. LServe demonstrates the compatibility of static and dynamic sparsity in long-context LLM attention. This design enables multiplicative speedups by combining these optimizations. Specifically, we convert half of the attention heads to nearly free streaming heads in both the prefilling and decoding stages. Additionally, we find that only a constant number of KV pages is required to preserve long-context capabilities, irrespective of context length. We then design a hierarchical KV page selection policy that dynamically prunes KV pages based on query-centric similarity. On average, LServe accelerates LLM prefilling by up to 2.9x and decoding by 1.3-2.1x over vLLM, maintaining long-context accuracy. Code is released at this https URL.

contents.AI: **LLM Inference.** Large Language Models (LLMs) are built upon transformer-based architectures characterized by a series of identical stacked layers, each integrating components such as attention blocks, feed-forward networks (FFN), and normalization elements. The process of LLM inference can be divided into two distinct phases: the initial prefilling stage, which is designed to manage multiple tokens simultaneously, and the subsequent auto-regressive decoding stage, where the processing is restricted to one token at a time for every request during the decoding step. **Attention.** The attention mechanism is critical for facilitating information exchange across tokens. It begins by transforming the input x through linear projections to create query vectors q ∈ RN×HD, along with key-value pairs k and v, both of which also reside in RN× ˆ HD, where ˆH denotes the count of key/value heads. In traditional multi-head attention (MHA), the number of heads is defined as H = ˆH. However, modern architectures (Touvron et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2023; 2024a) adopt a method known as grouped-query attention (GQA) (Ainslie et al., 2023), where H is set to n ˆH (n ∈ Z), thus effectively reducing the size of the KV cache. The current key (k) and value (v) are then concatenated with the KV cache derived from S preceding tokens, producing K and V matrices represented as R(S+N)× ˆ HD. The attention computation can subsequently be expressed by the following equations: Sh = qhKT ˆh √ D, oh = softmax (Sh) Vˆh, with ˆh = h n (1). This leads to the complexity of attention being articulated as LServe: Efficient Long-sequence LLM Serving with Unified Sparse Attention 3 (b) Latency breakdown of LLM decoding illustrated in the charts. As the input sequence length expands, the attention component increasingly predominates both stages because of its quadratic complexity during the prefilling stage and its linear complexity throughout the decoding stage. In contrast, the General Matrix Multiplication (GEMM) demonstrates linear complexity in the prefilling stage, exhibiting constant complexity during the decoding phase. The latency metrics were gathered using the Llama-3-8B model on an NVIDIA A100 GPU, revealing that the complexity is represented as O (N(S + N)HD), which escalates quadratically in the prefilling stage while increasing linearly during the decoding phase in relation to sequence length. In situations where S becomes considerable in length, both stages-decoding and prefilling-are chiefly constrained by the attention process. **Paged Attention.** When it comes to LLM serving, the length of generated sequences tends to be highly variable and difficult to predict. Applying padding to all sequences to reach a uniform maximum length can lead to significant memory waste and fragmentation issues. In response to this challenge, vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023b) has introduced an innovative approach called PagedAttention, a KV cache management strategy inspired by the principles of virtual memory used in operating systems. Rather than allocating a contiguous memory buffer for the KV cache of each sequence, PagedAttention segments the cache into fixed-size blocks, or pages, each of which is designated to store KV data for a specific number of consecutive tokens, typically ranging from 16 to 64. A page block table meticulously tracks the physical addresses of each page, enabling the PagedAttention kernel to utilize indirect addressing for the retrieval of KV features. Additionally, TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA, 2023) and QServe (Lin et al., 2024b) have implemented a quantized version of page attention, which serves to diminish memory bandwidth consumption during the decoding phase, thereby yielding further acceleration in the generation process.

contents.human: Serving long-sequence LLMs is challenging due to the high cost of attention. Figure 2 profiles the latency breakdown of Llama-3-8B with a batch size of 1 across various sequence lengths on the A100 GPU. In both the prefilling and decoding stages, attention kernels account for at least 50% of the runtime at sequence lengths over 64k, rising to 75% at 128k. According to QServe (Lin et al., 2024b), the ratio of attention kernels in end-to-end runtime will increase as the batch size scale up. Therefore, in real-world serving scenarios, optimizing the attention becomes increasingly critical. contents.AI: The task of serving long-sequence LLMs presents significant challenges, particularly due to the substantial computational expense associated with attention mechanisms. In Figure 2, we present a detailed latency analysis of the Llama-3-8B model, examining its performance with a batch size set to 1 for various sequence lengths while utilizing the A100 GPU. It becomes evident that during both the prefilling and decoding processes, attention kernels account for at least 50% of the total runtime when sequence lengths exceed 64k, with this figure escalating to as high as 75% at 128k. As reported by QServe (Lin et al., 2024b), the proportion of time spent on attention kernels within the overall end-to-end runtime is expected to rise as the batch size increases. This indicates that optimizing attention mechanisms is of paramount importance in practical serving environments. Effectively accelerating attention processes in long-sequence LLMs necessitates a profound understanding of how attention kernels are implemented on GPUs, as depicted in Figure 3. During the prefilling phase, each query token engages with all key and value tokens in a sequential, block-by-block manner. Implementing strategies to skip key-value (KV) blocks can substantially lessen the number of sequential iterations, thereby facilitating quicker attention computation. The parallelization of the attention kernel occurs across the dimensions of batch sizes, attention heads, and query tokens, with the decoding phase being restricted to a single query token per operation. Despite this parallelization, the calculations along the dimension of KV tokens remain inherently sequential. Within each iteration, a block-illustrated as a grid with an orange outline in Figure 3-is computed jointly by all threads within the current thread block. Though it is feasible to bypass certain calculations within each block, the resultant speedup is often negligible. This limitation arises from the lockstep execution model of threads inside a GPU warp, where faster threads must idle while waiting for slower ones to complete. Rather than concentrating on the sparsity within each individual iteration, a more effective strategy for accelerating attention computation revolves around minimizing the total number of sequential iterations along the KV token dimension. This leads to the introduction of our unified block sparse attention formulation, wherein attention operations are omitted in a block-wise fashion. In this architecture, with the exception of the most recently accessed KV block, each block is either computed in its entirety or completely omitted during the prefilling segment. Conversely, the decoding stage consists solely of one query token for each sequence, which decreases the dimensionality of each orange-contoured grid to a 1×P format, where P signifies the page size (i.e., the count of KV tokens within a given page). We will explore LServe’s approach to selecting sparsity patterns in further detail in Section 3. Moreover, in light of the fact that the decoding phase is often restricted by memory bandwidth, KV cache quantization also plays a vital role in enhancing speed. It’s important to note that quantization operates independently of block sparsity, as it contributes to a reduction in the runtime of individual iterations, while the focus of sparsity is to lower the number of iterations themselves. 3 LSERVE: LONG-SEQUENCE SERVING WITH UNIFIED SPARSE ATTENTION We present LServe, an innovative and efficient system designed for serving long-sequence LLMs with the incorporation of sparse attention mechanisms. Within LServe, various sparse attention patterns are cohesively integrated into a unified block-sparse framework, as depicted in Figure 4. This flexibility is realized through the use of fused CUDA kernels, which support diverse sparsity patterns. Additionally, LServe encompasses weight, activation, and KV quantization capabilities, which together led to a significant enhancement in generation throughput, particularly when processing shorter context lengths.

contents.human: As shown in Figure 3, skipping computations in the attention kernel by blockwise processing accelerates execution by shortening the sequential loop. Building on this, we introduce a unified block sparse attention pattern for both the prefilling and decoding stages: each thread block computes a TQ × TK tile (and TK × TV ) in parallel. Here, TQ > 1 in the prefilling stage and TQ = 1 in the decoding stage, with TK (or TV ) corresponding to the page size in PagedAttention (Kwon et al., 2023a). We define block sparsity in LServe as follows: for each TQ × TK tile in the attention calculation, it is either fully skipped (Figure 4(b), light gray blocks) or retained as in standard causal attention (Figure 4(b), blue blocks). Given that each GPU streaming multiprocessor can execute only a limited number of thread blocks simultaneously, the attention kernel execution time can be approximated by the total count of TQ × TK (and TK × TV ) blocks. With a block sparsity of r, where rN of the N total blocks are empty, the theoretical speedup from block sparse attention is 1/(1 −r). For example in Figure 4(b), 10 out of N=21 blocks are non-empty. Thus, the theoretical speedup ratio is 2.1×. Figure 4(c)(d) shows two sparsity patterns used in LServe. The first is streaming attention (Figure 4(c)), a specialized form of block-sparse attention where each token only attends to its immediate neighbors and initial tokens, known as attention sinks (Xiao et al., 2023). Unlike dense attention, where computation for each row scales with the token index, streaming attention keeps the computation for each token constant—in this case, only two local blocks and one sink block, as shown in Figure 4(c). This pattern is nearly costfree in applications with extremely long contexts. Because streaming attention follows a fixed pattern, we designate which heads use it in offline, and make it static for different input sequences in both prefilling and decoding. The second type of sparsity, illustrated in Figure 4(d), is page sparsity, which is specifically designed for the decoding stage where TQ = 1 applies to both skipped and selected pages. Unlike streaming attention, page sparsity in LServe is dynamic, allowing different query tokens to attend to different KV pages. As noted in Deja Vu (Liu et al., 2023), dynamic sparsity results in higher compression ratios than static sparsity. Our observations indicate that static sparsity offers up to a 2× efficiency gain, whereas dynamic sparsity bounds the decoding complexity to a constant, with each query attending only to a fixed number of KV tokens.
contents.AI: As illustrated in Figure 3, the process of skipping computations within the attention kernel through a blockwise processing approach enhances execution speed by effectively reducing the duration of the sequential loop. Building on this concept, we propose a cohesive block sparse attention framework that functions in both the prefilling and decoding phases: each thread block carries out a TQ × TK tile (and TK × TV) in parallel. In this context, TQ is greater than 1 during the prefilling phase, whereas TQ is equal to 1 in the decoding phase, with TK (or TV) representing the page size associated with PagedAttention (Kwon et al., 2023a). We characterize block sparsity in LServe in the following manner: for every TQ × TK tile involved in the attention computation, it can either be entirely omitted (as depicted in Figure 4(b), represented by light gray blocks) or preserved in accordance with standard causal attention (illustrated in Figure 4(b) with blue blocks). Given the constraint that each GPU streaming multiprocessor can operate on only a limited number of thread blocks simultaneously, the execution time for the attention kernel can be approximated by tallying the total number of TQ × TK (and TK × TV) blocks. When we introduce block sparsity denoted by r, where rN indicates the proportion of empty blocks out of the total N blocks, the theoretical enhancement in performance due to block sparse attention can be expressed as 1/(1 - r). For instance, as seen in Figure 4(b), out of a total of N=21 blocks, 10 are non-empty. Therefore, the theoretical speedup factor is calculated to be 2.1×. Figures 4(c) and 4(d) present two distinct sparsity configurations employed in LServe. The first is referred to as streaming attention (Figure 4(c)), which is a tailored version of block-sparse attention, allowing each token to exclusively focus on its immediate neighbors and on initial tokens, termed attention sinks (Xiao et al., 2023). Unlike dense attention, in which the computational effort for each row varies with the token index, streaming attention maintains a consistent computational effort for each token-specifically, engaging only two local blocks along with one sink block, as demonstrated in Figure 4(c). This approach is nearly cost-free when applied to scenarios involving exceptionally long contexts. Due to the predictable nature of streaming attention, we designate which heads will utilize it during offline configuration, thereby ensuring its static application across varying input sequences in both the prefilling and decoding processes. The second type of sparsity, as represented in Figure 4(d), is referred to as page sparsity, which has been meticulously formulated for the decoding phase, where TQ is set to 1 for both the skipped and selected pages. In contrast to streaming attention, page sparsity within LServe is dynamic, permitting different query tokens to engage with varying KV pages. As highlighted in Deja Vu (Liu et al., 2023), this dynamic sparsity yields superior compression ratios compared to its static counterpart. Our findings suggest that while static sparsity presents an efficiency boost of up to 2×, dynamic sparsity confines the decoding complexity to a constant, ensuring that each query attends exclusively to a predetermined number of KV tokens.

contents.human: We present an overview of LServe in Figure 5. Built on QServe, which natively supports quantized LLMs, LServe enhances the baseline system by introducing sparsity into both prefilling and decoding dataflows. The two-way paged KV cache serves as the bridge between these two stages. As discussed in Section 3.1, we statically partition the attention heads of a pretrained LLM into two groups: dense heads and streaming heads. Unlike conventional LLM serving systems, which maintain a single KV cache, we utilize separate KV caches for the dense and streaming heads. The KV cache for the streaming heads is organized similarly to the pages in QServe, with scaling factors and zero points stored immediately after the token features. Additionally, the KV cache for the dense heads includes key statistics that facilitate critical page selection during the decoding stage. In the prefilling stage, the key differences between LServe and conventional dense-attention LLM serving systems are twofold: (1) we replace the dense attention kernel with our unified block sparse attention kernel, and (2) we write back quantized KV features using two distinct kernels. In the decoding stage, our system incorporates dynamic attention sparsity. Rather than developing an entirely new dynamic sparse attention kernel, we decompose the problem into two components: (1) dynamic page selection and (2) a dense attention kernel with shorter page tables, where the shorter page tables are provided by the page selector. Notably, our page selector employs hierarchical paging and reusable page selection, enhancing both long-context accuracy and page selection efficiency. contents.AI: In Figure 5, we provide a comprehensive overview of LServe. This system is constructed on QServe, which inherently accommodates quantized large language models (LLMs). LServe significantly elevates the foundational framework by integrating sparsity into the data flows related to both prefilling and decoding stages. A pivotal feature of our architecture is the two-way paged key-value (KV) cache, which effectively links these two distinct phases of operation. As elaborated in Section 3.1, we conduct a static partitioning of the attention heads found in a pretrained LLM, categorizing them into two separate groups: the dense heads and the streaming heads. Unlike traditional LLM serving systems that typically utilize a singular KV cache, LServe innovatively employs distinct KV caches allocated for both dense and streaming heads. The organization of the KV cache designated for streaming heads mirrors the paging structure of QServe, wherein scaling factors and zero points are placed immediately following the token features. Furthermore, the KV cache allocated for the dense heads encompasses essential statistics that aid in making key decisions during the critical phase of page selection in the decoding process. During the prefilling phase, there are two notable departures from traditional dense-attention LLM serving systems with respect to LServe: (1) we substitute the conventional dense attention kernel with our advanced unified block sparse attention kernel, and (2) we employ two unique kernels to rewrite the quantized KV features. When it comes to the decoding phase, our system integrates dynamic attention sparsity into its operations. Instead of inventing an entirely new dynamic sparse attention kernel, we opt to dissect the issue into two primary components: (1) the process of dynamic page selection, and (2) a dense attention kernel that utilizes shorter page tables, where these shorter tables are supplied through the page selector mechanism. A particularly noteworthy aspect is that our page selector utilizes hierarchical paging alongside a reusable selection process, which substantially bolsters both the accuracy of long-context processing and the efficiency of page selection. **LServe: Efficient Long-sequence LLM Serving with Unified Sparse Attention** In the prefilling stage, LServe concurrently processes dense heads and streaming heads through a fused sparse attention kernel. Past keys and values are managed through two distinct paging systems-one devoted to streaming heads and the other to dense heads. During the decoding phase, LServe implements dynamic sparsity on the dense heads, utilizing a meticulous page selection procedure. Only those selected KV pages get loaded into the attention mechanism for the decoding stage. For clarity, we intentionally omit details such as normalization layers and residual connections from this figure.

contents.section_title: 3. LSERVE: LONG-SEQUENCE SERVING WITH UNIFIED SPARSE ATTENTION
contents.human: We adopt the approach from DuoAttention (Xiao et al., 2024) to classify each attention head as either a retrieval head or a streaming head. Using DuoAttention’s optimization-based identification method, we obtain a gating value α ∈[0, 1] for each head, where values closer to 1 signify a retrieval head, and values closer to 0 indicate a streaming head. To classify a head as a retrieval head, we compare α to a threshold τ, determined by a sparsity quantile. For instance, with a target sparsity of 50% across attention heads, τ equals the median of all gate values, thereby designating half of the heads as retrieval heads.
contents.AI: We implement the methodology presented in DuoAttention (Xiao et al., 2024) to categorize each attention head distinctly as either a retrieval head or a streaming head. By utilizing the optimization-based identification technique introduced by DuoAttention, we derive a gating value denoted as α ∈ [0, 1] for each individual head. In this context, gating values that are closer to 1 serve as an indication that the head functions primarily as a retrieval head, while values that trend towards 0 suggest that the head operates more as a streaming head. In the process of classifying a head as a retrieval head, we perform a comparison of α against a predefined threshold τ, which is established based on a sparsity quantile. For example, if we aim for a target sparsity of 50% across all the attention heads, we set τ to equal the median of all calculated gate values. This approach consequently results in the classification of half of the attention heads as retrieval heads.

contents.human: To effectively translate sparsity into performance gains, it is essential to avoid iterating over a complete sequential loop and relying on conditional statements to determine data loading and computation requirements. This method is inefficient for GPU computation patterns, which thrive on minimizing branching within loops. Instead, we should focus on iterating only over the necessary blocks by accurately calculating offsets to load data and assess whether a block should be processed. To facilitate this, we introduce an iterator-based abstraction that standardizes indexing operations. This allows us to loop exclusively over the blocks requiring computation, with data offsets easily computed using offset = iter(i + 1) −iter(i). This abstraction efficiently skips unnecessary blocks with minimal overhead and necessitates few changes to the kernel function, thus enhancing maintainability. Take the streaming heads as an example, the iterators are determined outside the attention kernel since streaming heads are configured offline and the attention pattern is fixed. Once the attention on sink tokens is complete, the iterator automatically updates the memory pointer to the first local token in the KV cache with minimal overhead. Additionally, our iterator-based formulation unifies the more general block sparse pattern (see Figure 4).
contents.AI: To truly translate the concept of sparsity into tangible performance improvements, it is crucial to move away from the practice of iterating through a complete sequential loop while depending on conditional statements to ascertain the requirements for data loading and computation. Such an approach is far from efficient when considering the computation patterns utilized by GPUs, which are designed to thrive on minimizing branches within loops. Instead, our focus should shift towards iterating solely over the blocks that are necessary, achieved through precise calculations of offsets to determine how to load data and to evaluate the need for processing a given block. To streamline this process, we propose an iterator-based abstraction that standardizes the operations involved in indexing. This innovation enables us to loop exclusively over the blocks that require computation, as data offsets can be easily calculated using the formula offset = iter(i + 1) -iter(i). This technique allows for the efficient bypassing of unnecessary blocks, incurring minimal overhead, and requiring only a few modifications to the kernel function, thereby improving maintainability. For instance, when considering the streaming heads, the iterators are defined outside the attention kernel, given that streaming heads are set up offline and the pattern of attention remains fixed. After the attention process on sink tokens has been completed, the iterator seamlessly updates the memory pointer to point to the first local token within the KV cache, all while maintaining low overhead. Furthermore, our iterator-based formulation serves to unify the broader block sparse patterns, as illustrated in Figure 4.

contents.AI: In order to further improve the decoding throughput for long-context large language models (LLMs), we propose the implementation of dynamic sparsity, which builds upon the input-agnostic static sparsity outlined in Section 3.1.

contents.AI: We note that the shortcomings of the query-aware KV cache selection paradigm, as depicted in Figure 6, do not stem from the coarser granularity associated with sparse attention (which corresponds to a larger page size). Instead, the primary issue arises from the fact that the statistical indicators at the page level become homogenized, making them less representative, especially when a single page contains an excessive number of tokens. To tackle this problem, we have developed a straightforward yet effective hierarchical paging system that incorporates an abstract layer of virtual logical pages to assess token criticality while maintaining the original physical memory structure of the KV cache. As demonstrated in Figure 7, our hierarchical paging approach organizes NL tokens into a logical page, while NP tokens are grouped into a physical page (where NP = g · NL, and g is an integer). In this setup, a single physical page accommodates g logical pages. The tokens within a specific logical page work collectively to contribute to the computation of a single criticality estimator. The results presented in Table 1 illustrate how page size significantly influences the efficiency of the LLM serving system: larger page sizes tend to be more favorable for hardware, as they enhance memory layout contiguity and optimize GPU bandwidth utilization during attention calculation. For instance, simply reducing the page size utilized by QServe (as noted by Lin et al., 2024b) results in a marked decrease in the performance of the end-to-end system. To illustrate this, we assess the per-step decoding latency (measured in milliseconds per step) of QServe running on a solitary A100 GPU for our analysis. We employ the Llama3-8B model architecture, using a batch size of 32. In the LServe system, we employ the channel-wise minimum and maximum key values from the logical pages as representative vectors; this method has been validated as an effective metric (according to Tang et al., 2024) when estimating page significance, particularly with a moderate page size (≤16). The current query is designed to engage with these representative vectors from each logical page to compute the corresponding importance scores, formulated as follows: Sj = D ∑ i max(q[i] ∗ k[j] max[i], q[i] ∗ k[j] min[i]) (2) Here, S represents the importance score of the logical page, j indexes the logical pages (where j can be a, b, etc.), i denotes the channel index, and D indicates the head dimension. The overall importance ascribed to each physical page is determined by applying a max-reduction method over the importance scores of its associated logical pages. Ultimately, LServe identifies the top-K physical pages (selected according to a predetermined token budget) that possess the highest importance scores to serve as input for the sparse attention kernel.

contents.human: One remaining question is: as physical page size increases, will the hierarchical paging require a higher token budget for sparse attention to retain accuracy? Given a generation step, assume the most important history tokens are distributed in a logical page set P = {P(i, j)}, where i ∈{1, 2, ...}, j ∈{a, b, , ...} are the physical and logical index of a page accordingly. If these important tokens are randomly and sparsely distributed in the context, chances are that all logical pages in P are scattered in different physical pages, that is, for any P1, P2 ∈P, i1 ̸= i2. In this case, all |P| physical pages (|P| · NP tokens) are selected to avoid losing important information. contents.AI: One important question that remains is whether an increase in physical page size will necessitate a higher token budget for hierarchical paging when utilizing sparse attention in order to maintain accuracy. In the context of a generation step, let us assume that the most crucial history tokens are organized within a logical page set P = {P(i, j)}, where $ i ∈{1, 2, …} $ and $ j ∈{a, b, …} $ represent the physical and logical indices of a page, respectively. If these significant tokens are dispersed randomly and sparsely throughout the context, it is likely that all logical pages within P are distributed across various physical pages, meaning for any two pages $ P1, P2 ∈P $, $ i1 ≠i2 $. In this scenario, all the physical pages |P| (which totals $ |P| ·NP $ tokens) must be selected to ensure that important information is not lost. However, the LServe: Efficient Long-sequence LLM Serving with Unified Sparse Attention feature suggests a complexity that must be addressed, as reflected in the following details. The hierarchical paging mechanism relies heavily on datasets that exhibit scattered entries, with implications articulated through mathematical quantifications such as $∑max(q[i] ·kmax[i], q[i] ·kmin[i])$. This formulation evaluates the importance associated with each token in the provided structured array of physical and logical pages. For instance, logical page distributions, demonstrated by vectors such as $ kmax $ and $ kmin $, showcase various importance scores across the pages. The physical page data reviewed reveals patterns in how logical pages-which have been allocated dimensional tokens, characterized in the figure representations-contribute to the overall efficiency of this modular structure. In addressing the potential drawbacks associated with na ̈ıve paging, where only $ |P| ·NL $ tokens are retained since it directly minimizes page sizes to smaller units (e.g., $ NL $), one must consider how hierarchical paging might lead to a diminished incidence of attention sparsity calculated by $ NP / NL $. Thankfully, the natural continuity found in semantic constructs of language bestows the attention operation with a fundamental locality, thereby enabling LServe to uphold a steady sparse attention token budget even when physical page sizes are expanded. During what is referred to as the decoding stage, the coherent arrangement of contextual tokens generally prompts the current query token to preferentially attend to succeeding pages residing in the KV cache. Consequently, logical pages with elevated significance scores are likely to cluster within physically proximate pages. This spatial locality considerably mitigates the urgency for a larger token budget, subsequently diminishing the overhead typically stemming from the tension between quantization practices and sparse attention efficiency. Empirical evidence illustrated in Figure 13 substantiates that our hierarchical paging effectively retains model accuracy, even when adhering to the same token budget as utilized with the standard page selector that incorporates smaller page sizes. Moreover, during the decoding process, the attention mechanism also demonstrates additional behavioral qualities characterized as temporal locality. This illustrates how adjacent query tokens consistently show a tendency to focus on similar historical pages. As a result, there is no requisite for queries at successive decoding stages to independently determine salient pages for selection. Instead, the decision-making process regarding page selection can be shared across queries-this aligns with the block-sparse attention design depicted in Figure 4(d). To support this operation, we introduce a concept labeled as Reusable Page Selection within LServe’s framework. In this illustration of Sparse Attention, the inefficiencies present in the Vanilla pipeline reveal the potential for enhancement through a Dynamic Page Selector. In contrast, our innovative reusable page selector takes advantage of the inherent similarity between queries relevant to consecutive tokens, aiming to diminish the selector overhead. The chunk size allocated for the reusable selector has been established at 2 for illustrative clarity. As demonstrated in Figure 8, we engage the page selector solely at the commencement of predefined chunks. For consecutive tokens contained within the same chunk, we apply the page selection findings derived from the initial token in that chunk. By leveraging the temporal sparsity of attention, this approach significantly boosts the speed of long-context generation while preserving accuracy. Illustrated in Figure 14, it is evident that while dynamic sparse attention serves to effectively constrain the complexity of decoding attentional constructs, the latency experienced by the page selector escalates linearly in relation to the sequence length. As the volume of historical tokens exceeds 64K, the na ̈ıve page selector inevitably becomes a bottleneck affecting system efficiency. In contrast, the implementation of our reusable page selector notably alleviates this critical problem, enhancing the overall operational efficacy of the framework.

contents.human: During the decoding stage, attention heads are processed in parallel on GPU, enabling different sparsity patterns to be applied independently on each head. This flexibility enables some heads to operate with page-level sparsity while others follow the streaming computation pattern. To leverage this, we employ a two-level indexing hierarchy to unify the operations for streaming heads and dense heads with dynamic sparsity. Specifically, the low-level (physical) index corresponds to the iteration step of current GPU thread, which executes in a consecutive manner as in dense attention, while logical index denotes the actual position of the target token within the entire KV cache. For each dense head, the page selector provides an index table to map physical index to logical index. Streaming heads are treated as dynamic sparse heads with index table only containing the sink and local pages. contents.AI: Implementation. We have developed LServe utilizing CUDA and PTX assembly, building upon the foundations established by QServe (Lin et al., 2024b) and the TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA, 2023) frameworks. The specialized CUDA kernels generated from this process are seamlessly compiled into PyTorch extensions, allowing for enhanced flexibility and compatibility with the entirely PyTorch-focused serving interface. Testbed. The primary experiments for our study were carried out on a powerful server outfitted with 8 NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs and 2 AMD EPYC 7763 CPUs, which collectively provide 128 processing cores and a robust 2TB of memory. Unless specifically indicated otherwise, all experiments harness the power of the A100 GPUs. Moreover, we also conducted a few evaluations on a cloud instance that features a single NVIDIA L40S 48GB GPU in order to analyze the performance of our system across varying GPU architectures. All evaluations were executed using PyTorch version 2.5.0 alongside CUDA 12.4 and cuDNN 9.2.0. Models. In order to thoroughly evaluate the performance of the system against different LLM architectures, we utilized the widely recognized GQA-based model Llama-3-8B (Dubey et al., 2024), along with the MHA-based model Llama-2-7B (Touvron et al., 2023), as well as the smaller-scale model Minitron-4B (Muralidharan et al., 2024). Furthermore, to enable long-context inference, we incorporated the context-extended version of Llama-3-8B, referred to as Gradient (Pekelis et al., 2024). Metrics. Our primary area of focus lies in serving throughput. For our evaluations presented in Table 3, we examined the accuracy of Llama-3-8B on the RULER benchmarks (Hsieh et al., 2024), which include intricate tasks such as multi-hop tracing and aggregation, designed to test the model’s behavior beyond mere context retrieval. The notation LServe-N indicates that the token budget allocated for dynamic sparsity is set to N. It should be understood that for long-context inputs, the latency experienced in LServe is not solely driven by attention mechanisms; contributions from the page selector and GEMM computations also play a significant role. Our experimental results indicate that LServe-8192 registers only a marginal increase in latency, being up to 6% slower compared to LServe-4096 when the sequence length surpasses 128K. The performance metrics for Llama-3-8B at sequence lengths of 32K, 64K, 128K, 160K, 192K, and 256K are as follows: Dense 90.5, 86.8, 83.8, 79.3, 79.6, 79.4; LServe-4096 91.0, 85.6, 81.0, 79.0, 76.1, 75.7; and LServe-8192 91.8, 86.1, 81.7, 81.2, 79.7, 79.1. During the prefilling stage, we prioritize time-to-first-token (TTFT) as a crucial metric, whereas in the decoding stage, our emphasis shifts toward minimizing latency associated with per-token generation. Baselines. In establishing our findings, we regarded several systems as baselines, utilizing their most recent versions to ensure the integrity of our comparisons. We enabled W8A8 precision for the baselines wherever it was attainable. These baselines include: • vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023b), recognized as one of the leading LLM serving systems that implements PagedAttention; • QServe (Lin et al., 2024b), an efficient LLM serving system which employs W4A8KV4 quantization; • MInference (Jiang et al., 2024b), the cutting-edge system tailored for accelerating long-context prefilling stages; • DuoAttention (Xiao et al., 2024), a robust framework designed for long-sequence LLM inference that incorporates static sparse attention. Additionally, we extend our comparative analysis to include the state-of-the-art system Quest (Tang et al., 2024), which excels in long-context decoding stage acceleration, although it exclusively supports MHA models. Consequently, we conducted and elaborated on this comparison in Table 4.
